title: WISE 0855−0714 (coldest known brown dwarf)
astrometry_source: Position: AllWISE designation 08h55m10.831s -07d14m42.53s as given in the challenge (reference epoch assumed 2010.5). Parallax and proper motion: Luhman & Esplin 2016, AJ 152, 78, Table 4 (0.449", -8.118, +0.680 "/yr).

story.hook: The coldest brown dwarf known, 7 light-years away. Watch it cross two arcminutes of sky since 2010.
story.what_to_look_for: The blink opens on WISE (2010) against SPHEREx (2026) at 4.4–5.0 µm, where cold brown dwarfs glow. The faint dot in the circle jumps about 21 pixels west (to the right). Between SPHEREx visits alone it moves about 1.3 pixels per year. In the short-wavelength bands (D1–D3) it is invisible; the light near the circle there is an ordinary star 7.8 arcseconds away that does not move.
story.what_it_is: WISE 0855−0714 is a brown dwarf about 7 light-years away, roughly as cold as Earth's North Pole in winter. It was found in 2014 because it moves fast across the sky in WISE images (about 8 arcseconds per year). It is almost invisible at short infrared wavelengths and gives off most of its light near 4.5 µm.
story.answer: WISE 0855 is the faint dot in the circle in the 3.8–5 µm bands; it shifts west by about 1.3 pixels per year. The steady star just beside it is an unrelated Gaia star (G = 16.3).
story.honest: This is near the limit of SPHEREx. In the 3.8–5 µm bands a faint source sits within about half a pixel of the predicted position and shifts west between SPHEREx visits by about the predicted amount, and from WISE (2010) to SPHEREx (2026) it moved a measured 20.7 pixels against 20.9 predicted. A third, independent test is colour: in frames without flagged pixels, the light in our measuring circle is 2.3 times higher at 4.4–5.0 µm than at 2.4–3.8 µm (552 ± 55 versus 243 ± 22 microjansky, a 5.2-sigma rise using the scatter between frames as the error), and the rise appears in each of the three visits. Ordinary stars get fainter toward 5 µm; cold brown dwarfs get brighter. Together, the 16-year motion, the positions and the colour make it very likely that the dot is WISE 0855 itself. The signal in single SPHEREx frames is weak, and an unrelated star 7.8 arcseconds away blends with it at 0.75–3.8 µm, where the light at the circle is mostly that star. For the same reason, its brightness chart is not reliable: the measuring circle includes part of the neighbouring star.

bands.label: 4.4–5.0 µm: thermal glow of cold brown dwarfs
